title: LLM Inference Optimization Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on how LLM serving works and how to make it fast: prefill vs decode, the KV cache, batching, quantization, speculative decoding, and the latency, throughput and time-to-first-token trade-offs.

chapters.title: Prefill vs Decode: The Mental Model
points: Prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel forward pass, so it is compute-bound and fills the KV cache
Decode generates one token per forward pass, reading all weights and the KV cache each step, so it is memory-bandwidth-bound
Autoregressive loop: each new token depends on the previous one, so decode steps cannot be parallelised within one request
Time to first token (TTFT) is roughly queue wait + prefill time; time per output token (TPOT) is the decode step time
Total latency = TTFT + (output tokens − 1) × TPOT, so long prompts hurt TTFT and long outputs hurt total time

chapters.title: The KV Cache
points: Attention needs the keys and values of every previous token; caching them avoids recomputing the whole prefix each decode step
Cache size per token = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes per value; it grows linearly with sequence length and batch size
Worked example: Llama-2-7B in FP16 uses about 0.5 MB per token, so a 4k-token sequence takes about 2 GB
GQA and MQA share KV heads across query heads to shrink the cache several times over
Paged attention (vLLM) stores the cache in fixed-size blocks, removing fragmentation and allowing prefix sharing
Common mistake: sizing GPU memory for weights only; the KV cache, not the weights, often caps batch size and context length

chapters.title: Batching and Continuous Batching
points: Decode is memory-bound, so batching many requests amortises one weight read across them and raises throughput almost for free
Static batching waits for the whole batch to finish, so short requests idle behind the longest one and GPU slots are wasted
Continuous (in-flight) batching schedules at every token step: finished sequences leave and queued requests join immediately
Chunked prefill splits long prompts into pieces mixed with decode steps, so one big prompt does not stall other users' tokens
Larger batches raise throughput but also per-request latency and KV cache use; the cap is GPU memory and the latency target

chapters.title: Quantization: INT8 and INT4
points: Quantization stores weights (and optionally activations or KV cache) in fewer bits: FP16 → INT8 halves memory, INT4 quarters it
Because decode is memory-bound, fewer bytes per weight gives faster tokens and lets a bigger model fit on one GPU
Weight-only INT4 (GPTQ, AWQ) is the common serving choice; INT8 weights and activations (SmoothQuant) also speed up compute-bound prefill
Quantization is lossy: INT8 is usually near-lossless, INT4 shows small quality drops, and outliers and small models suffer most
Common mistake: skipping evaluation after quantizing; always compare task accuracy and perplexity against the FP16 baseline

chapters.title: Speculative Decoding and Latency vs Throughput
points: Speculative decoding: a small draft model proposes k tokens, the large model verifies all k in one parallel pass and keeps the accepted prefix
Output distribution is unchanged because rejected tokens are resampled from the target model, so quality is lossless
Speedup depends on the acceptance rate: a poor draft model or high-temperature sampling gives little or negative gain
It helps low-batch, latency-sensitive serving; at large batch sizes the GPU is already busy and the gain shrinks
Latency vs throughput: bigger batches raise tokens per second overall but slow each user, so pick the batch size from the SLO (TTFT and TPOT targets)

chapters.title: LLM Inference Cheat Sheet
points: Prefill = compute-bound, sets TTFT; decode = memory-bound, sets TPOT
Latency = TTFT + (N − 1) × TPOT; KV bytes per token = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes
Batching: continuous > static; add chunked prefill to protect TPOT and cap batch by KV memory
Precision: FP16 → INT8 is 2× smaller, INT4 is 4× smaller; always re-evaluate quality
Speculative decoding: draft k tokens, verify in one pass, lossless; best at low batch with high acceptance
Interview Point: know how to lower TTFT (shorter prompts, prefix caching, chunked prefill) versus raise throughput (bigger batches, quantization)
